core: The paramountcy principle: engineering codes place the safety, health, and welfare of the public above the engineer's obligations to client and employer, and both NSPE and ASCE encode the ordering explicitly

The standing duties that surround the paramountcy principle: competence and practising only within one's area, objectivity and truthfulness in reports and testimony, disclosure of conflicts of interest, confidentiality and its stated limits, and sustainability obligations as they now appear in codes

Ethics is not the same as legality and not the same as civil liability; professional-conduct rules are enforced by state licensing boards and by professional societies, not by courts, and at least one code says in terms that it does not establish a standard of care

What the codes direct an engineer to do when professional judgment is overruled under circumstances that endanger life or property: notify, document, escalate, refuse to seal non-conforming work, and if necessary withdraw
Whistleblowing as a last resort: what the codes ask, what the personal cost has historically been, and how narrow and deadline-bound U.S. legal protection actually is

The canonical case literature verified against the investigations rather than the folklore: Challenger (Rogers Commission), Hyatt Regency walkways (NBS BSS 143 plus the Missouri licensing-board appeal), Ford Pinto (NHTSA recall plus the Grimshaw opinion), and Volkswagen diesel emissions (EPA notices and the federal criminal case)
Separating what an investigation established from what remains contested or is simply mis-remembered
supporting: Why the engineer's seal matters: in Missouri the seal carried statutory responsibility for the work, and the licensing board's revocation of two engineers' certificates was affirmed on appeal

Why the OSH Act's anti-retaliation provision is a weak backstop for engineers: a 30-day filing window, a complaint to the Secretary of Labor rather than a private suit, and a statute list that is industry-specific rather than general
The structural pattern the cases share: a documented technical concern moving upward through a decision structure whose incentives are not technical
outOfScope: Licensure mechanics, the FE and PE exams, ABET accreditation, and the structure of the profession — owned by engineering-fundamentals:engineering-thinking:what-engineers-do
Technical failure analysis, factors of safety, and failure modes — owned by engineering-fundamentals:engineering-practice:safety-factors-and-failure
The data-presentation and charting critique of the Challenger decision — owned by engineering-fundamentals:engineering-practice:engineering-communication
Legal advice, professional advice, or guidance on how any individual should act in a live employment dispute
Non-U.S. codes of ethics and non-U.S. regulatory regimes
Any position on a current or ongoing controversy or investigation

claims.claim: The NSPE Code of Ethics for Engineers opens its Fundamental Canons with a direction to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public, and separately directs engineers to act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees; the ordering of the canons and the elaboration in the Rules of Practice make the public duty the one that governs when the two collide.

The ASCE Code of Ethics groups an engineer's responsibilities under five stakeholders — society, the natural and built environment, the profession, clients and employers, and peers — states that in a conflict between ethical responsibilities the five stakeholders are listed in order of priority, and singles out the duty to protect the health, safety, and welfare of the public as taking precedence over all other responsibilities in the code.

The ASCE Code of Ethics carries a footnote stating that the code does not establish a standard of care and should not be interpreted as such, which keeps a professional-conduct rule distinct from the negligence yardstick a court applies.

Both codes impose the same cluster of standing duties around the public-safety principle: undertaking assignments only when qualified by education or experience and not signing or sealing documents in subject matter one lacks competence in; being objective and truthful in professional reports, statements, and testimony and including all relevant and pertinent information in them; disclosing known or potential conflicts of interest; and keeping a client's or employer's confidential business and technical information confidential.

Confidentiality under the NSPE code is bounded, not absolute: the rule against revealing facts, data, or information without the client's or employer's consent carves out disclosure authorized or required by law or by the code itself, and a separate rule directs engineers who know of an alleged code violation to report it to appropriate professional bodies and, when relevant, to public authorities. The ASCE code likewise directs engineers to report misconduct to the appropriate authorities where necessary to protect the health, safety, and welfare of the public.

Sustainability appears in the two codes with different force. The NSPE code places it among Professional Obligations as an encouragement to adhere to the principles of sustainable development in order to protect the environment for future generations, with a footnote defining sustainable development as meeting human needs for resources, energy, food, transport, shelter, and waste management while conserving environmental quality and the natural resource base. The ASCE code makes the natural and built environment its second-ranked stakeholder, with duties to adhere to the principles of sustainable development, to consider and balance societal, environmental, and economic impacts, to mitigate adverse effects, and to use resources wisely while minimising resource depletion.

The codes give explicit direction for the moment when judgment is overruled. NSPE directs that if engineers' judgment is overruled under circumstances that endanger life or property they shall notify their employer or client and such other authority as may be appropriate; that engineers shall approve only engineering documents in conformity with applicable standards; and that engineers shall not complete, sign, or seal plans or specifications not in conformity with applicable engineering standards, and shall notify the proper authorities and withdraw from the project if a client or employer insists. ASCE directs engineers to present clearly and promptly to clients and employers the consequences when engineering judgment is overruled where public health, safety, and welfare may be endangered.

Professional societies can discipline members, but the authority that can end a person's right to practise belongs to state licensing boards. The NSPE code itself records that state registration board rules of professional conduct are not affected by the antitrust judgment against the society and remain in full force and effect, and NCEES describes licensure as a state and territorial board mechanism directed at protecting public health, safety, and welfare.

Licensing-board discipline for professional-conduct failures is real and can be career-ending. After the Hyatt Regency collapse the Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors filed a complaint in February 1984; the Administrative Hearing Commission found the certificates subject to discipline under Sec. 327.441 RSMo 1978, the Board ordered the engineering certificates of Daniel Duncan and Jack Gillum and the certificate of authority of G.C.E. International revoked, the trial court affirmed, and the Missouri Court of Appeals affirmed in Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. Jan. 26, 1988).

The Duncan court recorded the specific conduct found: Duncan was found grossly negligent in the preparation and completion of a structural drawing and in failing to review shop drawings, and guilty of misconduct for representing a connection as safe while ignorant of its safety because the engineering tests and calculations had not been performed; Gillum was found responsible for Duncan's acts and omissions by having affixed his professional seal to the structural drawings, grossly negligent in failing to review or assure review of that drawing before sealing it, and guilty of misconduct over an atrium design review he did not perform. The Commission defined gross negligence in the licensing context as an act or course of conduct demonstrating a conscious indifference to a professional duty — different in kind from ordinary negligence, not merely in degree.

The National Bureau of Standards concluded that the most probable cause of the July 17, 1981 Hyatt Regency walkways collapse was insufficient load capacity of the box beam-hanger rod connections, with failure initiating at the connection on the east end of the fourth floor walkway's middle box beam, and identified two contributing factors: inadequacy of the original connection design, which was identical for all three walkways, and a change in hanger rod arrangement during construction from one continuous rod set to two sets, which essentially doubled the load on the fourth floor connections.

NBS quantified how deficient the connections were: the maximum load on a fourth floor box beam-hanger rod connection at the time of collapse was only 31 percent of the ultimate capacity expected of a connection designed under the Kansas City Building Code, and had the original hanger rod arrangement not been changed the ultimate capacity would have been approximately 60 percent of that expected under the code — so the as-drawn design was already below code expectation before the construction change.

The casualty figure for the Hyatt Regency collapse differs between the two authoritative records: NBS BSS 143, issued May 1982, reports 113 dead and 186 injured, while the Missouri Court of Appeals in 1988 states that 114 people died and at least 186 were injured. Both describe it as the most devastating structural collapse to take place in the United States in terms of loss of life and injuries.

The Rogers Commission concluded that the cause of the Challenger accident was the failure of the pressure seal in the aft field joint of the right Solid Rocket Motor, and that the failure was due to a faulty design unacceptably sensitive to temperature, physical dimensions, the character of materials, the effects of reusability, processing, and the reaction of the joint to dynamic loading.

The Commission recorded that the ambient temperature at launch was 36 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 degrees lower than the next coldest previous launch, and that the coldest point on the right aft field joint, at the 300-degree circumferential position, was estimated at 28 plus or minus 5 degrees Fahrenheit.

In the January 27, 1986 teleconference, Thiokol engineers including Roger Boisjoly presented low-temperature O-ring concerns and Robert Lund's charts, and Boisjoly testified that the conclusion was that they should not fly outside their data base, whose low point was 53 degrees. Thiokol's Joe Kilminster initially told NASA he would not launch; Thiokol then requested an off-net caucus and reversed its recommendation.

The Rogers Commission's findings on the decision process were that there was a serious flaw in the decision making leading up to the launch of 51-L; that the waiving of launch constraints appears to have been at the expense of flight safety; that Marshall management showed a propensity to contain potentially serious problems and resolve them internally rather than communicate them forward; and that Thiokol management reversed its position and recommended launch at the urging of Marshall and contrary to the views of its engineers in order to accommodate a major customer.

The concern was documented internally and in writing long before the launch. On July 31, 1985 Boisjoly wrote a memorandum to R. K. Lund, Thiokol's Vice President of Engineering, warning that if a nozzle-joint scenario recurred in a field joint the result would be a catastrophe of the highest order and loss of human life, and recommending a dedicated team. A launch constraint imposed in July 1985 was then waived six consecutive times before 51-L, and the Commission found that neither the constraint, the reason for it, nor the waivers were known to the Level I and Level II managers during the 51-L flight readiness process.

The Commission also found that a careful analysis of the flight history of O-ring performance would have revealed the correlation between O-ring damage and low temperature, that neither NASA nor Thiokol carried out such an analysis, and that tracking only anomalies outside the prior flight data base allowed major problems to be removed from and lost by the reporting system.

NHTSA recall campaign 78V143000, received June 19, 1978, covers Ford Pinto passenger vehicles and describes a fuel-system defect in which a rear impact could disconnect the fuel filler pipe from the tank or puncture the forward face of the tank, resulting in fuel leakage that in the presence of an ignition source could cause a vehicle fire and serious injury; the remedy was a longer filler pipe with an improved seal and a polyethylene shield on the front of the tank.

In Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (Cal. Ct. App. May 29, 1981), the court recited evidence that Pinto styling placed the fuel tank behind the rear axle with only 9 or 10 inches of crush space; that mechanical prototypes struck from the rear at 21 miles per hour and a production Pinto crash tested at 21 miles per hour into a fixed barrier suffered tank puncture or filler-neck separation; and that identified fixes ranged from about $2.10 to $9.95 per car, with a package of reinforced rear structure, smooth axle, improved bumper and added crush space costing about $15.30. The court also stated that when a prototype failed the fuel system integrity test, the standard of care for engineers in the industry was to redesign and retest it.

The document popularly called 'the Pinto memo' — the Grush-Saunby Report — was excluded from evidence at the Grimshaw trial; the appellate opinion says so expressly while rejecting Ford's complaint about counsel's reference to it. What was in evidence were different Ford documents, including exhibit 125, a 'Fuel System Integrity Program financial review' discussed at an April 1971 product review meeting, which recommended delaying the addition of a flak suit or bladder on affected cars until 1976 for a stated design cost saving of $10.9 million over 1974-1975.

The Grimshaw jury awarded Richard Grimshaw $2,841,000 compensatory and $125 million punitive damages, reduced by stipulation to $2,516,000 compensatory; on Ford's motion for a new trial Grimshaw was required to remit all but $3.5 million of the punitive award as a condition of denial of the motion.

EPA issued a notice of violation to Volkswagen on September 18, 2015 covering 2.0 litre diesel vehicles of model years 2009 through 2015 and a second notice on November 2, 2015 covering 3.0 litre diesel vehicles; software installed on the vehicles detected when a car was undergoing emissions testing and turned full emissions controls on only during the test, so that on-road emissions of nitrogen oxides reached up to 40 times the standard for the 2.0 litre vehicles and up to nine times the standard for the 3.0 litre vehicles.

On January 11, 2017 Volkswagen AG agreed to plead guilty to three criminal felony counts and to pay a $2.8 billion criminal penalty for a scheme to sell approximately 590,000 diesel vehicles in the United States using a defeat device to cheat on emissions tests mandated by EPA and the California Air Resources Board, and by lying and obstructing justice to further the scheme; in separate civil resolutions of environmental, customs, and financial claims VW agreed to pay $1.5 billion, for $4.3 billion in total.

Individual employees were prosecuted alongside the company. The federal criminal case in the Eastern District of Michigan captioned United States v. Liang, No. 2:16-cr-20394, records a judgment as to Volkswagen AG entered in April 2017, a government sentencing memorandum and sentencing hearing in August 2017 as to Volkswagen engineer James Robert Liang, and a judgment as to Oliver Schmidt entered in December 2017.

There is no single general federal statute protecting an engineer who reports a safety problem. OSHA's Whistleblower Protection Program administers the anti-retaliation provisions of a list of separate federal statutes — 25 as listed on the program's statutes page in August 2026 — each tied to a particular industry or subject matter such as aviation, rail, pipelines, nuclear energy, food safety, environmental media, consumer products, motor vehicles, or securities, and each with its own filing deadline.

The general workplace anti-retaliation provision is narrow and fast-expiring. Under section 11(c) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, 29 U.S.C. 660(c), an employee who believes he has been discharged or discriminated against may, within thirty days after the violation occurs, file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor; it is then the Secretary who brings any action in federal district court. OSHA's implementing regulation adds that complaints not filed within 30 days will ordinarily be presumed untimely, that tolling is available only on recognised equitable principles or in strongly extenuating circumstances, and that pending grievance-arbitration proceedings or a filing with another agency do not justify tolling.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many people died in the Hyatt Regency walkways collapse.
positions: NBS Building Science Series 143, issued May 1982, states 113 dead and 186 injured.
The Missouri Court of Appeals in Duncan (1988) states that 114 people died and at least 186 were injured.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both figures are reported in the lesson with their sources rather than one being picked silently. The NBS number is the count as of the May 1982 report; the higher figure appears in the later judicial record. Neither source explains the difference, so the lesson does not invent one.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a Ford cost-benefit memo drove a decision not to fix the Pinto.
positions: The popular account treats the 'Pinto memo' as the document in which Ford priced human lives and chose not to repair the car.
The Grimshaw opinion states that the Grush-Saunby Report was excluded from evidence, so the jury that returned the punitive award did not see it.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says only what the opinion establishes: the famous memo was not in evidence, and a different internal document (exhibit 125, a fuel system integrity financial review recommending deferral of a flak suit or bladder for a stated $10.9 million saving) was. The lesson labels the popular version as contested rather than repeating or refuting it beyond the record.

positions: The folklore version has NASA managers overruling an engineer's objection.

The Commission found that Thiokol management reversed its own engineering recommendation at the urging of Marshall and contrary to the views of its engineers, and separately found that neither the launch constraint nor its six waivers were known to the Level I and Level II NASA managers during the 51-L readiness process.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the Commission: the reversal was made by the contractor's management under customer pressure, and senior NASA management was not in possession of the relevant history. This is a more useful lesson about reporting chains than the folklore version.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing factual about engineering ethics at all; it consisted of subject-agnostic boilerplate ('Engineering Ethics is a foundational concept in Engineering Fundamentals', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') with no sources, no cases, no codes, and no distinction between ethics, law, and liability. All of it was discarded.
The draft's learning objectives, vocabulary, worked example, and question bank were generic placeholders and were replaced entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the whole generated draft with sourced content.

Corrected an earlier unverified working draft for this topic that stated the Rogers Commission's conclusion as 'a combustion gas leak through the right Solid Rocket Motor aft field joint ... initiating vehicle structural breakup'. That sentence is a finding in the accident-analysis sequence; the Commission's stated Conclusion to Chapter IV is that the cause was the failure of the pressure seal in the aft field joint of the right Solid Rocket Motor, due to a faulty design unacceptably sensitive to named factors. The lesson uses the Commission's own Conclusion.

Corrected the count of statutes administered by OSHA's Whistleblower Protection Program: the earlier working draft said 23; the program's statutes page lists 25 as of the August 2026 check. The lesson states the number with the check date attached because the list changes.

Corrected the Challenger temperature framing: 36 degrees Fahrenheit ambient was 15 degrees lower than the next coldest previous launch; 53 degrees Fahrenheit was the low point of the O-ring engineering data base, not the previous coldest launch temperature. The two numbers are separate and are easy to merge into a single wrong sentence.

Corrected the Hyatt attribution: the collapse is often told as a fabricator's rod change alone, but NBS found the original connection design was already at approximately 60 percent of code-expected capacity, so the change made an already-deficient design far worse rather than spoiling a sound one.

Dropped the Ford/Firestone tread-separation material carried in the earlier working draft. It is a genuine product-safety case but not part of the engineering-ethics case canon this lesson is scoped to, and including it diluted the lesson.

Dropped the earlier working draft's reliance on paywalled business-ethics articles and a blocked case-law aggregator for the Pinto demythologising point. The point is now carried by the appellate opinion itself, which states that the Grush-Saunby Report was excluded from evidence.

Added the Missouri licensing-board appeal, which the earlier working draft did not have. It is the strongest available primary demonstration that professional-conduct rules are enforced by a licensing board rather than a court, and it supplies the court's definition of gross negligence in the licensing context.
rightsIssues: The NSPE and ASCE codes of ethics are copyrighted publications of their societies with no reuse licence offered. Both are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY. The lesson describes what the codes require in its own words and quotes only two short attributed phrases that cannot be paraphrased without losing their meaning ('hold paramount' and 'faithful agents or trustees'). No canon, rule, or section is reproduced.

Engineering standards referenced inside the sources (for example the AISC Manual of Steel Construction and the Kansas City Building Code) are described by name and function only. No standard text, table, or design value is reproduced, and the lesson states no allowable stress, load factor, or design value.

U.S. court opinions and federal agency publications used here are U.S. government edicts or federal works and are treated as public domain. The Caselaw Access Project static files were used as a reading copy for two opinions; the canonical citation and a stable public opinion page are recorded in each source record.
NCEES web content carries no stated reuse licence and is REFERENCE_ONLY, reused at the id and URL already in the phase-1 source registry.

sourceRecords.title: NSPE Code of Ethics for Engineers
sourceRecords.notes: Existing phase-1 registry record, reused at the same id and URL. Retrieved the official PDF with a browser user-agent (the HTML page 403s) and read the full document: Preamble, six Fundamental Canons, Rules of Practice 1-5, Professional Obligations 1-11, the footnote defining sustainable development, and the appended antitrust statement. Supports the paramountcy principle and the faithful-agent canon; the competence, truthfulness, conflict-disclosure and confidentiality rules; the bounded nature of confidentiality; the overruled-judgment and refusal-to-seal directions; the sustainability encouragement; and the statement that state registration board rules of professional conduct remain in full force and effect. Copyrighted NSPE publication marked 'as revised July 2019'; only the phrases 'hold paramount' and 'faithful agents or trustees' are quoted, with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: Code of Ethics
sourceRecords.notes: Official three-page ASCE code PDF, downloaded with a browser user-agent and read in full. Supports the five-stakeholder priority ordering (society; natural and built environment; profession; clients and employers; peers), the statement that in a conflict the stakeholders are listed in order of priority with the public health-safety-welfare duty taking precedence over all other responsibilities, the footnote that the code does not establish a standard of care, the environment stakeholder's sustainability duties, the client-and-employer duties on conflicts of interest and confidentiality, the duty to present clearly and promptly the consequences when engineering judgment is overruled, and the duty to report misconduct to appropriate authorities. Copyrighted ASCE publication; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Licensure
sourceRecords.provider: National Council of Examiners for Engineering and Surveying (NCEES)
sourceRecords.notes: Existing phase-1 registry record, reused at the same id and URL as the merged what-engineers-do topic, which owns licensure as a subject. Re-fetched and re-read during this pass. Cited here only for the narrow point that NCEES's members are the 69 engineering and surveying licensing boards of the states, the District of Columbia, and the territories, and that the page describes licensure as existing so that individuals practise in a manner that protects the health, safety, and welfare of the public. That is the institutional fact that makes a state board, rather than a court or a society, the body able to end a right to practise; the disciplinary mechanics themselves are sourced to the Duncan opinion, not to this page. No reuse licence stated on the site; facts used, wording not reproduced.
